name: Bone grafting for lengthening

lead: Bone grafting for lengthening means opening a gap in a cut bone and filling it with bone taken from the patient (often the hip or fibula) or from a donor, then fixing it with a plate or pins. The bone ends up longer, so the limb or digit is longer. In looksmaxxing discussions it comes up as an alternative or add-on to gradual limb lengthening for people who want extra height or proportion.

Research is mostly orthopedic: reviews of foot and metatarsal lengthening describe grafts used in one-stage procedures for modest gains, with gradual distraction (the Ilizarov method) used for larger ones. Little has been published on grafting for cosmetic height.

paras: In the surgical literature, a surgeon cuts the bone, opens the gap to the planned length, places a graft (autograft from the iliac crest or fibula, or allograft) and fixes it with a plate or K-wire. The alternative, gradual distraction, adds new bone slowly with an external or internal device and sometimes receives a graft or biologic to help the gap heal (consolidate). Recovery involves months of protected loading and follow-up imaging.

Reported problems include graft resorption, nonunion or delayed union, infection, soft-tissue and nerve stretch when lengthening is large, hardware failure, and pain at the graft donor site. Reviews of foot lengthening describe one-stage grafting as generally limited to small gains (around 15 mm in that setting). China's health ministry banned limb lengthening in 2006 after operations caused serious side effects.

angle.text: The graft holds the bone at a longer length once it heals, so the added length is part of the skeleton rather than something worn. Surgeons describe it for modest gains, while larger gains are typically done with gradual distraction, sometimes with graft or biologic support.

lead: Bone grafting for lengthening is a family of orthopedic and craniofacial techniques in which a gap is created in a bone and filled or supported with graft material so that the bone ends up longer. The graft can be the patient's own bone (autograft, commonly from the iliac crest or fibula) or donor bone (allograft). It can be used for the whole gain in one operation, or as a supplement to gradual distraction when new bone in the gap needs help to consolidate.[1][2]

In appearance terms, the technique matters wherever a longer or better-proportioned bone changes how someone looks: leg or foot length for height and proportion, finger or thumb length after injury, jaw or chin length in facial surgery. In looksmaxxing forums it is discussed alongside limb lengthening as one of the surgical routes to extra height, with posters weighing the shorter treatment course of grafting against the greater lengthening distances of distraction.[3]

Published research is largely reconstructive. A 2025 review of foot lengthening compares one-stage grafting with the Ilizarov method, and case reports describe grafting in thumb reconstruction and in lengthening after bone cysts or congenital defects.[1][4][5] No trial has tested grafted lengthening as a cosmetic height procedure.

paras: In a one-stage graft lengthening, the surgeon cuts the bone, separates the ends to the planned length at once, places a graft in the gap and fixes the construct with a plate or pins. The review of foot procedures describes grafts from the iliac crest or fibula or from donors, and notes that this route is generally considered safer for shortening below about 15 mm and is often chosen when appearance is a priority.[1]

Distraction osteogenesis works differently: the bone is cut, there is a latency period of about a week, the ends are then separated about 1 mm a day, and the new bone consolidates while a device holds the position.[2][6] Grafts and biologics such as bone morphogenetic protein have been explored as additions to this approach.[6]

The foot-lengthening review sets out the trade-off. One-stage grafting offers a shorter treatment course but is limited in how far it can lengthen and carries a risk of graft resorption. Ilizarov distraction allows greater lengthening and is more established but takes longer and has pin-tract infection, joint stiffness, nonunion and refracture among its reported complications. The authors note that combining the two can be useful and that Ilizarov is preferred above about 15 mm.[1]

Reported outcomes in the review include a first-metatarsal series of five patients with a mean gain of 1.7 cm and bony union by 12 weeks, and a fibular-graft series with a mean gain of about 9 mm and no complications at two years.[1]

Reported issues with grafted lengthening include graft resorption and soft-tissue problems, and a lengthening beyond about 25% of original length may raise tendon tension and stretch neurovascular structures.[1] Distraction series report infection in roughly 5% of cases, bone healing in the wrong direction in 7 to 9%, and hardware failure in 3 to 4.5%.[6]

Cosmetic limb lengthening has drawn regulatory and media attention. In 2006 China's Ministry of Health banned limb lengthening after operations caused serious side effects, and reports from India describe young patients with infections, smaller gains than expected and understated risks.[2]

Posters on T Nation have discussed lengthening of other bones, including clavicle lengthening by distraction, citing case series on congenital cases while noting those patients already had deformities.[3] Discussion tends to treat grafting as one option within the wider hardmaxxing category of surgery for height and structure.

No studies have tested bone-graft lengthening as a cosmetic height procedure. Related reconstructive literature includes a 2025 review of foot lengthening comparing one-stage grafting with the Ilizarov technique,[1] a case report of thumb lengthening with an iliac crest graft and a forearm flap, which achieved near-contralateral length,[4] and a case report of grafting and lengthening for a recurrent femoral bone cyst.[5] Registered trials have examined artificial bone graft in calcaneal lengthening for flatfoot in children[7] and relapse after mandibular lengthening.[8]

timeline.event: Bernhard von Langenbeck first proposes gradual bone lengthening.[6]
Alessandro Codivilla publishes first clinical attempts in 26 people; complications are high.[6]
Gavriil Ilizarov develops external fixators and sets distraction rates, leading to widespread use.[6]
